/us-news/2026/sep/24/xi-jinping-trump-ch.headline: Xi Jinping calls for extensive US-China cooperation and regular military dialogue at White House summit with Trump
/us-news/2026/sep/24/xi-jinping-trump-ch.bodyHtml:
Xi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington, setting out how the US and China can avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put them on a military collision course amid rising tensions over artificial intelligence, trade and Taiwan.

The Chinese president laid out terms for a mutual understanding that he said could steer the two competing superpowers on to a road of mutual gain and away from future military conflict, at the start of his summit meeting with Donald Trump in the White House.

Xi said the goal should be conditions for “achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again go hand in hand”, rather than confrontation, citing Trump’s political catchphrase.

“We should strengthen communication. China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialog, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” said Xi, with Trump looking on.

“We should coexist in peace,” he said. “China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialog and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.”

With such conditions in place, Xi said, “the Thucydides trap can be overcome” – a reference to the phenomenon, defined by the Greek historian, of tensions that arise when an emerging power challenges the dominance of an established power.

Xi invoked the phrase in his meeting with Trump in Beijing in May, asking the US president how he planned to avoid it.

Xi’s proposals for lessening tensions also included the invitation of 100,000 young Americans to visit China on student exchanges. They come amid a period of intense competition between the two powers over artificial intelligence and trade, with each side imposing tariffs on the other.

Addressing Trump directly, Xi said: “During your visit to China this year, we agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability. I am ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course towards the future.”

Xi also extolled his personal relationship with his American counterpart, saying: “President Trump and I have respect for each other. We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.”

Trump had earlier welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House, noting that he was the first Chinese leader to make a second state visit to the US. The previous visit took place in 2015, when Barack Obama was US president.

“President Xi and Madame Peng arrive at an important moment for America, the 250th anniversary of our founding,” he said.

Trump said that he had forged “a truly great friendship” with Xi. “President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries,” he said. “Our teams have been working to encourage a more balances trading relationship, including the new market access for American farmers and ranchers.”

He said the current visit would include discussion over security, technology and AI – which he called “super intelligence”, a term he introduced in his speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday.

The White House welcome ceremony followed Trump’s unusual step of going to Andrews air force base in Maryland the evening before to greet the Chinese leader and his wife on the tarmac.

Much of the same pageantry was repeated in Thursday’s ceremony, with both countries’ national anthems being played. Trump was flanked by his wife, Melania, while members of his cabinet and senior aides – including Natalie Harp, Trump’s dedicated assistant nicknamed “the human printer” by fellow staffers – looked on.

Trump and Xi were scheduled to hold bilateral talks after the ceremony and the welcoming speeches.

Both leaders adopted a harmonious tone, though analysts have voiced scepticism about the possibility of longstanding stable arrangements being arrived at over a host of issues.

A truce agreed between Trump and Xi in South Korea last year aimed at keeping tariffs lower, which had been due to expire in November, has now been extended until February, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said.

Analysts believe the extension suggests Trump continues to be dissatisfied with Xi’s concession offers on trade and wants to keep the pressure on in the hope of getting a better deal if the two meet again at the G20 summit scheduled to be held in Miami in December.

In the race for AI, the US has placed strict export controls on microchips, semiconductors, software and chipmaking equipment in a bid to slow China’s development.

Chinese imports have continued to surge into the US despite the trade war between the two countries. China is on course to run a $1tn trade deficit for the second year running.

• The headline and text of this article were amended on 24 September 2026 to correct a misspelling of Xi Jinping.

/media/2026/sep/24/bbc-doom-spiral-cuts-.headline: Journalists’ union and TUC press government to step in for the BBC as Brittin holds weekly funding talks
/media/2026/sep/24/bbc-doom-spiral-cuts-.bodyHtml:
At the TUC conference last week, delegates passed a motion instructing the body to press the government to intervene over cuts to public service broadcasters.

Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, is holding weekly meetings with the government over the BBC’s future funding model – at the same time as making the cuts and battling staff over pay.

The BBC has been warned it risks entering a “doom spiral” of endless cuts and weaker public support for its services, as insiders anticipate the imminent closure of some TV and radio services.

Morale at the corporation is said to be extremely low as a series of cuts are slowly revealed to staff. In the latest announcement, the BBC said it would be reducing the number of local specialist correspondent roles.

It immediately triggered concerns about the loss of expert, local knowledge. The cuts are part of a plan to save £500m and shed up to 2,000 jobs.

Staff are now expecting announcements over the closure of programmes to follow next week. Brittin has been open with staff for several months that popular shows would have to go, to ease the broadcaster’s mounting financial pressures.

There has been speculation that the BBC Three channel could be closed for the second time in its short history. BBC Three, which launched shows including Fleabag and This Country, was moved online in 2016 before the decision to take it off television was reversed in 2022.

BBC radio output is also likely to be affected. Between 350 and 400 hours of audio content will be cut by the end of the next financial year.

BBC Local staff have now been told the corporation would be reducing the number of specialist correspondent roles. Instead, there will be “two dedicated, multi-platform correspondents in every BBC region”.

Earlier this week, staff at BBC Sport were told that 36 more jobs were going, including some senior production journalists.

Staff morale had already been hit by a series of cuts announcements this year. In June, it said there would be 550 job cuts in news, nations and TV and radio content. It included the end of Radio 4’s The World Tonight after more than 50 years.

In a comprehensive statement on the cuts, the National Union of Journalists said they risked locking the BBC into producing worse content and lower public support for the licence fee that funds it.

“The BBC’s ongoing campaign of cuts is devastating and demoralising for our members and severely undermines the broadcaster’s ability to serve audiences across the UK,” said Laura Davison, general secretary of the National Union of Journalists. “The latest wave of cuts piles on the misery already being felt.

“The more cuts the BBC makes, the more its services suffer. This makes it more difficult for the broadcaster to justify public spending, which in turn leads to further cuts. The BBC is at risk of entering an inescapable doom spiral if it continues in this direction.

“This is where the UK government must step in. The BBC has been undermined by years of underinvestment and interference.”

Senior management roles are also being reduced, with 10 per cent of “senior leaders” going. About 700 roles are expected to go across the BBC’s corporate divisions.

/world/2026/sep/24/france-says-eus-made-.headline: Germany and Nordic countries back UK inclusion in EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ law
/world/2026/sep/24/france-says-eus-made-.bodyHtml:
Germany and Nordic countries are backing a broader approach that would include the UK in the EU’s “Made in Europe” policy, while France is leading a push to exclude the UK that could result in British companies losing out in the race to supply European countries with low-carbon technologies and electric cars.

Andy Burnham raised the plans when he met the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, on the sidelines of the UN general assembly earlier this week.

The policy, still under negotiation, aims to protect European companies from intense and “unfair” state-subsidised competition from China. Resolving the issue has become one of Burnham’s top priorities for the EU-UK relationship, with the government fearing British companies risk being collateral damage.

One key EU proposal is the Industrial Accelerator Act, which would require authorities spending public money – awarding subsidies or public contracts – to favour European products in sectors such as renewable technologies and electric cars.

Germany wants a broader “Made with Europe” policy that would include the UK and other allies. Germany’s economic affairs minister, Katherina Reiche, told her counterparts: “We must reduce unilateral and critical dependencies, but we must not isolate ourselves from the rest of the world. This means that partner countries must be included in the union-origin principle, in general and on the condition of reciprocity.”

This position gets broad support from Nordic countries, which traditionally favour open trade.

Sweden’s outgoing deputy prime minister, Ebba Busch, who leads on business policy, said “we always miss the Brits”. Sweden wanted “a good solution where there is balance, given that some European countries are not members of the European Union but still completely essential for a functioning European market” she added.

One EU diplomat said it was a “big risk” if the UK government were to insist on a deal at an autumn summit. “It puts [the UK] in a corner, because this [Made in Europe criteria] is a process that is very difficult for the EU27 [to agree internally]”.

Ireland, which is chairing EU ministerial negotiations, hopes for an agreement in December on the IAA, including the Made in Europe provisions, between the EU Council and the European parliament. “There are a divergence of views on the Industrial Accelerator Act, on European preference, on working with trusted partners and third countries,” said Ireland’s enterprise minister, Peter Burke. “It is difficult, but we have a pathway in sight.”

Poland’s economic development minister, Michał Baranowski, said it was too early to say whether countries such as Switzerland, the UK, Japan, Australia and Canada would be in or out, adding: “All these countries are in the mix of the discussion.”

The UK, he said, should have clarity on its status when the EU act is passed, he said, adding: “We are in the last stretch, but this last stretch might take a while.”

A UK government spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and trusted European partner, committed to our shared security and economic cooperation.

“We will continue to engage with the EU on Made in Europe and work together, as like-minded partners, to boost growth and open up trade.”

But there is an intense debate inside the EU on how to define “made in Europe” and how far to include countries such as the UK, Canada and Japan.

France pushed for a narrow definition, starting with the EU27, at a meeting of EU industry ministers in Brussels on Thursday.

“European taxpayers’ money should support [European] workers and European factories”, the French industry minister, Sébastien Martin, told reporters. Asked about the UK, he said: “The United Kingdom made a choice a few years ago to leave the European Union. That doesn’t mean that we don’t discuss things or that we don’t trade, it doesn’t mean that there can’t be agreements in certain sectors, but fundamentally there are those who have chosen the European project and those who have decided to leave.”

France’s Europe minister, Benjamin Haddad, speaking in London, had few assurances to offer the Burnham government either. Asked about the risks of pushing the EU’s like-minded trading partners away, Haddad said: “At the end of the day, if you are not part of the internal market and if you are not contributing to the financial capacity of the internal market, you don’t get the same kind of protection.”

The charged internal EU27 debate on Made in Europe raises questions about the timing of the EU-UK reset summit, which was postponed when Keir Starmer stood down as prime minister. Since Burnham took office, no date has been fixed for the talks which are meant to happen in 2026.

British officials expect the summit will take place in November, although an earlier 6 November date has been scratched out. By December the EU is expected to be embroiled in deeply difficult internal negotiations on the bloc’s next seven-year budget, which are likely to consume the political bandwidth of EU leaders.

EU insiders believe that a Made in Europe agreement is a top priority for the UK, but have cautioned this cannot happen before the union has finalised its own position.

/technology/2026/sep/24/construction-lar.headline: Nscale clears Essex site and explores onsite power for UK’s ‘largest AI supercomputer’
/technology/2026/sep/24/construction-lar.bodyHtml:
The builder of a huge datacentre project hailed by the UK government has cleared its site and is investigating onsite power and a faster grid connection, though the project will miss its launch date next year and could be delayed into the mid-2030s.

Nscale said it was “committed to the project”, and the scaffolding yard site has now been cleared by the company. Nscale is also investigating whether it can generate power onsite and whether it can speed up the connection process, though the failure to find a quick fix to the power supply issue underlines how much energy has become a hindrance to datacentre development.

Keir Starmer’s government cited the Loughton project when announcing the UK’s AI strategy in 2025, describing the site as the “largest UK sovereign AI datacentre”. Datacentres are the central nervous system of AI technology such as chatbots.

The site in Loughton, Essex, was described as the country’s largest AI supercomputer when it was announced in 2025, but power supply problems mean it now faces a lengthy wait before coming online.

The Loughton site is seeking up to 90MW of capacity, equivalent to the energy consumption of about 315,000 homes.

The Loughton supercomputer is being built by Nscale, a UK-based startup seeking a $35bn (£26bn) flotation this year. There are now further concerns about the project due to its inability to obtain enough power before its planned 2027 debut.

Doubts had already emerged about the scheme after the Guardian revealed in March that the planned location was still an operational scaffolding yard.

UK Power Networks (UKPN), the company that will connect the site to the local power grid, has reportedly told Nscale the grid will not be able to supply sufficient power to the datacentre until the early to mid-2030s.

The power delay was first reported by Morning Intelligence, an AI industry newsletter.

Ofgem, the energy industry regulator, has warned of a logjam in applications for electricity connections. In June, it revealed there were 315 datacentres queueing to connect to the National Grid, representing 73GW of demand – compared with the peak energy demand for the entire country of 45GW.

UKPN said it could not comment on an individual project. Schemes with large energy demand also require work to be done at a National Grid level, in order to ensure that energy demands can be met properly.

“In general, many datacentres, whilst they will connect to our distribution network, are awaiting works on the wider national electricity transmission network before they can begin operation,” said a UKPN spokesperson.

National Grid said: “We’re continuing to work closely with NESO [the government-owned National Energy System Operator], distribution network operators and customers to identify opportunities to accelerate connections where possible and support economic growth.”

/politics/2026/sep/24/rory-stewart-stran.headline: Rory Stewart’s four-second gaze of absolute focus becomes a much-shared Newsnight meme
/politics/2026/sep/24/rory-stewart-stran.bodyHtml:
Rory Stewart has been an Afghan NGO leader, a Conservative leadership candidate, a Harvard professor, a popular podcaster, and the deputy governor of an Iraqi province.

This week, he created a moment that drew wider attention than any of them: he fixed a beady gaze on a fellow Newsnight panellist for the longest four seconds in television history.

Stewart, who now co-presents The Rest Is Politics podcast with Alastair Campbell, appeared on the BBC programme on 18 September – but in the last few days, a clip of the moment in question has taken on a life of its own on social media.

Stewart appeared alongside the former Labour leader Neil Kinnock and the New Statesman’s political editor, Ailbhe Rea, to discuss the day’s main news stories, including the race between China and the US to develop artificial intelligence (AI).

After Stewart made his comments, the presenter Matt Chorley asked Rea what Westminster could do about the development of AI. Stewart then swivelled around in his chair and stared directly at the journalist with an expression – and posture – of absolute focus.

Chorley told the Guardian the behaviour had not appeared overly strange in person: “I didn’t notice Rory looking particularly intently at anyone during the course of the programme,” he said.

He only became aware of what had happened when several friends texted him. “You know a moment from Newsnight has cut through when friends and family who don’t normally watch it are suddenly sending me clips,” he said. “But it is just quite a funny moment.”

He added that as it was the first Newsnight episode to move to the programme’s new earlier slot at 7pm, it had been “quite manic” in the runup. He had even joked to the panellists: “Anything that can be used to go viral, maybe a punchup or whatever, a tiff at the table, if you want to do that, that’d be great.”

Chorley observed that Stewart was “used to this”, after another clip of him taking his tie off during a Tory leadership debate had gone viral in 2019.

“It’s not the first time that something he’s done has gone wild online. I think he was genuinely probably just intently listening to what Ailbhe had to say. But there was something about the camera angle and his very direct look,” he said.

Many behaviours that appear normal in person can look strange on screen, Chorley added.

He said he had learned to “remember you’re always on” and to control his naturally emphatic hand movements, which can “look crazy” on screen. He also recalled an early Newsnight episode which had surprised viewers when Tim Stanley, a columnist at the Telegraph, winked at the camera.

“This is just the beauty of live telly,” he said. “It’s a reminder that even when the camera is on the person who’s talking, you might be in shot.”

Rea, who was on the receiving end of the stare, posted the clip on X to joke that she would “please like attention levels like this on my latest interview” after sharing a link to her most recent reporting.

The clip has turned into a meme online, with commenters imagining situations in which the stare could have taken place.

The Larry the Cat social media account posted: “When HR tells you that you need to listen better to female colleagues.”

Total Politics Group’s chief executive, Mark Wallace, compared Stewart’s behaviour to the comedian Kevin Eldon’s surreal style, writing: “There’s a high degree of Kevin Eldon energy to this. Magnificently strange.”

/music/2026/sep/24/macklemore-free-pales.headline: Macklemore takes Free Palestine tour to Dublin, Paris and London to raise funds for humanitarian causes
/music/2026/sep/24/macklemore-free-pales.bodyHtml:
Macklemore has announced a “Free Palestine” tour: a series of live shows in which the US rapper will perform alongside musicians and friends to raise funds for humanitarian causes in Palestine.

The list of organisations the concerts will benefit has been shared: Anera, Glia, Gaza Soup Kitchen, Taawon, Heal Palestine, Palestinian Youth Movement, Middle East Children’s Alliance, Jewish Voice for Peace, Medical Aid for Palestinians, Institute for Middle East Understanding, Palestine Children’s Relief Fund and UNRWA USA.

According to a press release, these organisations “represent the array of work in support of Palestinian people. That includes medical care, humanitarian assistance, education, community support, advocacy, organising and media work connected to Palestinians.”

The announcement comes after Macklemore (AKA Benjamin Haggerty) was removed from Ed Sheeran’s US stadium tour after he called for a “free Palestine” onstage and said he wanted the people of Gaza and “the occupied West Bank” to know “we have not forgotten about them”.

In response to the speech, made on 4 September, venue owners refused to allow any concerts featuring Macklemore to take place on their property.

Alongside his tour announcement, Macklemore posted on Instagram: “If these last couple of weeks have shown us anything, it’s that something has shifted over the last three years. There has been a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now.

“It’s 2026. Being apolitical during a genocide doesn’t work anymore. People are asking artists to show up, educate themselves and be in community. To use the stage for more than entertainment. To push back when the call for a Free Palestine is met with attempts to silence it.

“What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage. When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention.”

Macklemore’s statement continued: “So, as you all know, my schedule freed up a bit.” He said he had been using his time to contacts “artists who have shown up and used their stages to stand in solidarity with the Palestinian people, regardless of the consequences. Artists who understand that our platforms mean very little if we’re only willing to use them when it’s safe.”

Further lineup details for Macklemore’s tour are yet to be released.
“Because of how quickly all of this has come together, a lot of the conversations, schedules and details are still being worked out,” he wrote. “But this is a moment of momentum, and there is work to be done.”

In a written statement, Sheeran responded to the backlash over Macklemore’s removal, declining responsibility for the decision and saying: “I am not complicit.”

Irish songwriter Aaron Rowe, Billie Eilish’s older brother Finneas and Danish band Lukas Graham – all Sheeran’s remaining support acts – subsequently dropped out of the tour, alongside the Irish trad group Beoga, who were to accompany Sheeran for portions of the show.

Sheeran returned solo to the stage in Philadelphia on 19 September and read an apology about “making mistakes” from a teleprompter. “I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet,” he said.

Other concertgoers said they were sticking by the musician, while small groups of fans protested outside the venue, with some of them having sold their tickets in protest. A tearful Sheeran told the crowd: “Everyone is telling me to cancel, and I’m feeling all of my friends and family and people I know abandon me and I look at the end of the week and I see 50,000 people who haven’t abandoned.”

According to data from Social Blade reported by the Independent, Sheeran is estimated to have lost almost half a million followers across social media in the days since the controversy kicked off.

Macklemore’s tour will begin in Dublin on 26 October. Two of Sheeran’s former support acts are Irish, and many Irish musicians have been outspoken in their support for the Palestinian people, citing their own country’s history of occupation and oppression, as Rowe did in his statement explaining his departure from Sheeran’s tour:

“As Irish people, we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation,” Rowe wrote. “I need to be true to myself and my ancestors who resisted colonisation, and fought for a freedom that I enjoy today in Ireland.”

Dates in Paris (29 October) and London (30 October) have also been announced, with North American dates to follow. Fans hoping to get tickets are encouraged to sign up for presale access at macklemore.com.
